author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

text:
We should ban people from vibe coding RTL against a commercial VIP to demonstrate AI can design chips.

If you burn enough tokens, you can reverse distill the behavior of the VIP back into RTL form. AI is very good at copying, but that's not how silicon design works in reality.

It sets unrealistic expectations for the real RTL/DV engineers

comments.text:
Curve fitting RTL to match the VIP?

Design and Verif should be requirement spec based in my view. There is a tendency to get the design to match the Verif without a spec. Then, there is no single source of correctness. This can lead to wrong designs that pass verification, as many of us have seen in our careers.

author.name: Rob Taylor
author.headline: Old hand of Open Source. Expert in: - OSS IC design tools, with Open and Proprietary mfg processes - Embedded system engineering with OSS - AI agent creation - Networking - GPU acceleration Open to interesting opps

replies.text:
Jeremy Ralph agreed, if you're using AI for rtl, a solid system for requirements tracking, plans and architecture decisions is a prerequisite. Then you want to have multiple harnesses available for generation and validation.

A great way to gain more confidence in rtl generation is to build two implementations from the spec, your real, performant one, and a really dumb one, and use formal equivalence checking.

author.name: Zolboo Naranbaatar
author.headline: Building deterministic infrastructure for hardware review and AI agent execution · Ark Axiom · Ark Sovereign

comments.text:
Rob Taylor and Horace Chan are describing the most dangerous side effect of the current AI hardware hype: Correlated Vacuity.

When an LLM "vibe codes" RTL by reverse-distilling a VIP, it learns to write logic and assertions that perfectly mirror its own architectural blind spots. The simulation passes, the coverage dashboard turns green, but the system has merely verified a vacuous state space. It is an illusion of correctness.

Rob Taylor is spot-on that formal equivalence is the necessary backstop. However, throwing un-audited, AI-generated RTL directly at a formal solver almost guarantees state-space explosion and timeouts.

A diff is not a review answer. We don't need more generative tools; we need Review Compression. We must use deterministic graph analysis to run Bounded Triage—isolating the exact logic cones where Semantic Drift occurred.

By delivering a Cryptographic Handoff of those localized boundaries, we give senior DV engineers the exact, constrained targets they need to run those formal equivalence checks in minutes, rather than wasting weeks debugging probabilistic noise.

author.name: Horace Chan
author.headline: Expert in applying AI in verification

replies.text:
Zolboo Naranbaatar The industry probably has to go much deeper. What is a specification? what exactly is a bug and what is a feature?

Why write a spec in ambiguous English language when we can enlist the help of AI to write a formal spec that can feed into AI at the PCIe SIG level.

Think of the spec as an API, each company can compete on the implementation in term of gate area, power, latency, throughput extra, but their implementation has to formally proved meet the contract of the protocol.

Here is the best part, PCIe SIG can adopt the business model of SQLite, the English spec is free, the formal AI readable spec need to pay.

I can think of a couple of approaches, but I think the important thing in all of these is to drive *from* the requirements breakdown to minimise compounding of hallucinations/errors

author.name: Dr. Tobias Ludwig
author.headline: CEO | Formal Verification Enthusiast | Building the leading systemized Formal Verification delivery partner for the semiconductor industry

comments.text:
True, we should be careful what we celebrate as progress.

Demos that equate "copied VIP behavior" with "designed a chip" set unrealistic expectations for RTL/DV teams and blur the line between engineering and mimicry.
Imagine buying that IP and talking to their customer support when problem arises.
